reviewBoundary: Three whole fifteen-gap senior originals: fictional library and rehearsal cases plus general sound explanation. All keys and alternatives reviewed by same author; no independent calibration.

units.title: The chair beside the window
units.alignmentNote: One complete original fifteen-gap four-choice passage following National I response structure. The reference supplies level/family only, not prose.

materials.title: The chair beside the window
materials.text:
When the library replaced its old chairs, I offered to help attach small labels showing where each new chair belonged. Most were identical. One, however, had a higher seat and a ____1____ back. It attracted comments immediately.

I placed that chair in a quiet corner, thinking I was keeping the main room ____2____. The librarian asked why. When I explained, she said the chair had been ordered for readers who found the lower seats difficult. Its difference was its ____3____, not a fault to hide.

We moved it beside a table near the window. Then I prepared a label saying "special chair". The librarian paused again. A reader might need the higher seat without wanting a public ____4____ about it. Could the label explain the feature rather than describe the person?

I wrote "higher seat, firm back" instead. We added the same factual descriptions to our seating ____5____, which showed the different chairs available. The information let readers choose without asking them to tell us a personal ____6____.

Over the following week, several people used the chair. One was recovering from an injury; another simply ____7____ its height. Nobody needed to prove that their reason was more ____8____ than someone else's. If the chair was free, it could be used.

I had begun the job treating identical appearance as the main ____9____ of a well-arranged room. Now I noticed that a room could look orderly while offering too few ____10____. Putting every different object out of sight made the difference harder to ____11____, but did not remove the need it served.

Before finishing, I checked that the route to the window table was ____12____. The useful chair would be little help if other furniture blocked it. I attached the final label and stood back. Nothing looked dramatic. One chair was simply ____13____ where it could be found and reached. That was a small change in the room, but a larger change in what I ____14____ by ready for ____15____.

questions.prompt: Choose the best word or phrase for blank 1.
questions.explanation: Firm names the functional back later repeated on the label. Broken/missing/invisible would not describe the new supportive chair.

questions.prompt: Choose the best word or phrase for blank 2.
questions.explanation: The narrator is preserving identical appearance, hence uniform. The room is neither cleared, locked nor moved outdoors.

questions.prompt: Choose the best word or phrase for blank 3.
questions.explanation: The difference serves its intended purpose. Price/owner/colour are not the reason for the higher seat.

questions.prompt: Choose the best word or phrase for blank 4.
questions.explanation: A special label publicly announces a personal difference. Refund/argument/concert do not describe disclosure by the label.

questions.prompt: Choose the best word or phrase for blank 5.
questions.explanation: A seating guide provides available features. Bills/ceilings/uniforms do not normally provide this information resource.

questions.prompt: Choose the best word or phrase for blank 6.
questions.explanation: Readers need not disclose their personal history. Password/recipe/timetable do not name the private reason for choosing a chair.

questions.prompt: Choose the best word or phrase for blank 7.
questions.explanation: Another reader chooses the height by preference. Repair/measurement/painting do not supply the stated reason for sitting.

questions.prompt: Choose the best word or phrase for blank 8.
questions.explanation: No ranking of deserving reasons is required. Cost/distance/colour do not express entitlement to the free seat.

questions.prompt: Choose the best word or phrase for blank 9.
questions.explanation: Identical appearance was taken as a sign of a well-arranged room. Noise/cause/expense do not fit this criterion claim.

questions.prompt: Choose the best word or phrase for blank 10.
questions.explanation: Different seating offers choices. Windows/labels/volunteers are not the limited range of seats being discussed.

questions.prompt: Choose the best word or phrase for blank 11.
questions.explanation: Hidden difference is harder to notice. Carry/repair/purchase do not describe becoming aware of it.

questions.prompt: Choose the best word or phrase for blank 12.
questions.explanation: The next sentence contrasts a blocked route, so clear. Steep/wet/private do not address obstructions.

questions.prompt: Choose the best word or phrase for blank 13.
questions.explanation: The chair is placed accessibly. It is not invented, folded or sold in this closing action.

questions.prompt: Choose the best word or phrase for blank 14.
questions.explanation: The narrator changes the meaning intended by ready. Hearing/spending/forgetting do not fit the interpretation of that statement.

questions.prompt: Choose the best word or phrase for blank 15.
questions.explanation: The library is ready for its readers. Storage/painting/delivery are not the use the accessible arrangement supports.

units.title: Why a room answers back
units.alignmentNote: One complete original fifteen-gap four-choice passage following National I response structure. The reference supplies level/family only, not prose.

materials.title: Why a room answers back
materials.text:
A handclap in an empty hall may seem to produce a second clap. The sound can travel to a hard surface and return after being ____1____. What we hear depends partly on the room around us.

In a small room, the returning sound may arrive too quickly to seem ____2____ from the original. In a larger space, a sufficiently delayed reflection may be heard as an echo. Several surfaces produce returns at different times, creating a more ____3____ pattern than a single repeated sound.

Soft materials often absorb more sound than bare hard surfaces. Curtains and upholstered seats can therefore ____4____ how a hall sounds. This is one reason an empty rehearsal may differ from a performance with an audience. Listeners are not simply ____5____ the sound; their presence also changes the surroundings through which it travels.

That does not mean the quietest possible room is always the best. A musician may value some reflected sound, while a spoken announcement needs words to remain ____6____. Its purpose matters when judging its ____7____.

A class investigating this can compare recordings made at different positions, but the comparison needs care. Moving the microphone, changing its settings and altering the sound source all at once makes it difficult to ____8____ which change produced a difference. Keeping a record of the arrangement is therefore part of the ____9____, not merely paperwork afterwards.

A recording is also not identical to the experience of every listener. A listener can turn or move; a fixed microphone records from one ____10____. Its result is evidence about that arrangement, not a complete ____11____ of the whole hall.

Echoes connect everyday experience with design. The walls do not merely form a ____12____ boundary around an event. They help shape how it is heard. Understanding that relationship allows us to ask more ____13____ questions than whether a room sounds good or bad. We can ask good for what, heard from where, and under which ____14____. The returning clap becomes a starting point for ____15____, rather than an answer in itself.

questions.prompt: Choose the best word or phrase for blank 1.
questions.explanation: The returning sound is reflected from a surface. Translation/recording/silencing do not explain its physical return.

questions.prompt: Choose the best word or phrase for blank 2.
questions.explanation: A quick return is not perceived as a separate event. Loudness/age/safety do not name temporal distinction.

questions.prompt: Choose the best word or phrase for blank 3.
questions.explanation: Multiple return times give complexity. They do not guarantee permanence, music or privacy.

questions.prompt: Choose the best word or phrase for blank 4.
questions.explanation: Materials affect sound by absorbing it. They do not measure, advertise or describe the hall.

questions.prompt: Choose the best word or phrase for blank 5.
questions.explanation: Listeners receive sound as well as alter the environment. The other verbs assign unsupported production/commercial/language roles.

questions.prompt: Choose the best word or phrase for blank 6.
questions.explanation: Spoken words need to be intelligible. Novelty/secrecy/lack of recording do not define successful announcements.

questions.prompt: Choose the best word or phrase for blank 7.
questions.explanation: Acoustics names a space’s sound properties. Ownership/location/capacity are not what the examples evaluate.

questions.prompt: Choose the best word or phrase for blank 8.
questions.explanation: Controlled comparison identifies the cause. Ignoring/repeating/preventing changes does not name attributing a difference.

questions.prompt: Choose the best word or phrase for blank 9.
questions.explanation: Documenting settings belongs to an investigation. Decoration/audience/instrument do not name the whole comparative process.

questions.prompt: Choose the best word or phrase for blank 10.
questions.explanation: A fixed microphone records from one physical position. Opinion/generation/frequency do not describe where it sits.

questions.prompt: Choose the best word or phrase for blank 11.
questions.explanation: One recording is not a complete description. It is not discussed as a replacement person, owner or barrier.

questions.prompt: Choose the best word or phrase for blank 12.
questions.explanation: Walls form a visible/visual boundary as well as affecting sound. Financial/legal/weekly are not the spatial boundary in question.

questions.prompt: Choose the best word or phrase for blank 13.
questions.explanation: Purpose/position/conditions make questions precise. Politeness/urgency/privacy are not the refinement discussed.

questions.prompt: Choose the best word or phrase for blank 14.
questions.explanation: Arrangements and audience conditions change hearing. Instructions/names/prices do not complete the controlled-setting question.

questions.prompt: Choose the best word or phrase for blank 15.
questions.explanation: The clap begins inquiry. It need not be applause, create silence or begin building work.

units.title: The note nobody played
units.alignmentNote: One complete original fifteen-gap four-choice passage following National I response structure. The reference supplies level/family only, not prose.

materials.title: The note nobody played
materials.text:
During rehearsal for a small ensemble concert, violinist Nora stopped at the same bar three times. The phrase kept losing its ____1____. Each player was arriving at the next beat a little differently.

They slowed the passage and played carefully, but the problem ____2____. Then the pianist pointed to a short rest before the melody returned. They had concentrated on the sounds and treated the silence as an ____3____ space between them.

The rest was brief, but it belonged to the phrase. One player held the previous note too long; another started preparing the new one too early. Their sounds were accurate in ____4____, yet the shared timing had come apart.

They tried an unusual exercise: tapping the pulse and speaking only at the moment where the rest began. There was less to play, so it became easier to hear the ____5____ in their counting. The exercise did not replace musical expression. It gave them a shared point from which expression could ____6____.

On their next attempt, the melody returned without the earlier ____7____. They marked the place for another check at full ____8____. A success in slow practice did not automatically survive every change.

At the concert, nobody applauded the rest alone. It was not an isolated ____9____. Its contribution lay in the relationship between what came before and after.

Afterwards, Nora wrote in her practice journal. She had assumed that improving a performance meant giving more attention to the notes she ____10____. Now she included the moments when she had to listen without producing a sound. Silence could require as much ____11____ as a difficult run of notes.

She did not turn this into a rule that less playing was always better. The lesson was more ____12____: the page included different kinds of musical events, and her attention had been ____13____ distributed among them, favouring the audible notes. Once the group noticed the neglected rest, they could work on it together. The improvement came from hearing a ____14____ they had previously passed over, not from adding anything ____15____ to the score.

questions.prompt: Choose the best word or phrase for blank 1.
questions.explanation: The phrase loses coherent shape as timing diverges. Volume, authorship and instrument loss are not described.

questions.prompt: Choose the best word or phrase for blank 2.
questions.explanation: Careful notes did not solve timing; it remained. It did not disappear, spread to new places or reverse.

questions.prompt: Choose the best word or phrase for blank 3.
questions.explanation: They mistook silence for empty space. It was written rather than extra, no price is involved and silence is not an audible note.

questions.prompt: Choose the best word or phrase for blank 4.
questions.explanation: Sounds are individually accurate, in isolation. Advance/public/writing do not contrast individual accuracy with group timing.

questions.prompt: Choose the best word or phrase for blank 5.
questions.explanation: The stripped exercise exposes differences in counting. Instructions/instruments/compliments are not discrepancies in pulse.

questions.prompt: Choose the best word or phrase for blank 6.
questions.explanation: A shared basis lets expression develop. Retirement/disappearance/escape do not state the positive musical function.

questions.prompt: Choose the best word or phrase for blank 7.
questions.explanation: The return now lacks the earlier hesitation. Melody and the written silence remain; no notation is removed.

questions.prompt: Choose the best word or phrase for blank 8.
questions.explanation: Full speed is the changed condition after slow practice. Length/membership/price are not the tempo check.

questions.prompt: Choose the best word or phrase for blank 9.
questions.explanation: The rest contributes relationally rather than as an isolated effect. It is neither invitation/failure nor a physical instrument.

questions.prompt: Choose the best word or phrase for blank 10.
questions.explanation: She previously attended to notes she played. Printing/buying/translating are not her rehearsal actions.

questions.prompt: Choose the best word or phrase for blank 11.
questions.explanation: Listening through silence requires concentration. Equipment/applause/permission do not name the attentional effort.

questions.prompt: Choose the best word or phrase for blank 12.
questions.explanation: The lesson is specific rather than a universal less-is-better rule. Popularity/musical nature/cost do not express this narrower scope.

questions.prompt: Choose the best word or phrase for blank 13.
questions.explanation: Favouring audible notes explicitly shows uneven distribution of attention. Equally contradicts the preference; publicly/financially do not describe how attention is allocated to event types.

questions.prompt: Choose the best word or phrase for blank 14.
questions.explanation: They hear the before/rest/after relationship. No new soloist, praise or recording explains the repair.

questions.prompt: Choose the best word or phrase for blank 15.
questions.explanation: No new score content is added. Some existing content is difficult/quiet/written, so those alternatives do not express unchanged content.
